title: Cell Adaptation, Injury, Pigmentation, and Neoplasia
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows a cell from stress to adaptation, to reversible injury, to death, and in some tissues to neoplasia. It covers hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, and metaplasia; the mechanisms of injury that converge on ATP depletion, calcium overload, and oxidative damage; the patterns of necrosis and the pathways of apoptosis; the pigments and deposits that record past events in a tissue; and the features that separate a benign tumor from a malignant one. Board questions describe a microscopic change or a clinical setting and ask for the mechanism behind it, so each pattern here is tied to the process that produces it.
prerequisites: Oxidative phosphorylation, the electron transport chain, and anaerobic glycolysis
Cell cycle control by cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases, and the G1 to S checkpoint
Membrane transport, especially the Na+/K+-ATPase and calcium handling
Normal epithelial histology: stratified squamous, pseudostratified ciliated columnar, and simple columnar
Innate and adaptive immunity, including macrophage function and cytotoxic T cell killing

connections.to: Skin histology and the epidermal barrier (IN-1, IN-2)
connections.how: Callus, actinic keratosis, and melanocytic lesions make the epidermis the easiest place to see hyperplasia, dysplasia, and neoplasia in sequence.
Necrosis releases danger signals that start acute inflammation, while apoptosis is cleared silently, which explains why only one of the two leaves a scar.
Fas ligand, TNF, and perforin with granzyme are the immune system's routes into the apoptotic machinery, and PD-L1 expression is how tumors shut that machinery off.
Coagulative necrosis of the myocardium, dystrophic calcification of atheromas and valves, and metastatic calcification in chronic kidney disease are the same mechanisms in other organs.

connections.to: Biochemistry of free radicals and antioxidants
connections.how: Superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, and vitamins C and E limit the lipid peroxidation that drives both membrane injury and lipofuscin formation.

terms.def: An increase in cell size from added structural protein and organelles, without an increase in cell number.
Replacement of one mature differentiated cell type by another, through reprogramming of stem or reserve cells rather than transformation of mature cells.
Disordered proliferative growth with cytologic atypia and loss of normal maturation and orientation, still confined by the basement membrane.
Functional and structural change that resolves if the stress is removed, marked by cell swelling and fatty change with intact membranes.
A high-conductance channel in the inner mitochondrial membrane whose opening collapses the proton gradient and ends ATP synthesis.
Partially reduced oxygen derivatives, including superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radical, that oxidize lipids, proteins, and DNA.
Cell death in living tissue with loss of membrane integrity, enzymatic digestion of the cell, and leakage of contents that provokes inflammation.
Regulated, caspase-mediated cell death in which the cell shrinks and fragments into membrane-bound bodies that are phagocytosed without inflammation.
Deposition of calcium salts in dead or damaged tissue while serum calcium is normal.
Deposition of calcium salts in otherwise normal tissue because the serum calcium-phosphate product is raised.
Lack of differentiation, shown by pleomorphism, large hyperchromatic nuclei, a high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, and atypical mitoses.
Growth of tumor implants discontinuous with the primary tumor, the single feature that establishes malignancy.

sections.title: Cellular adaptations and the path to dysplasia

blocks.text: A cell under persistent stress can change its size, its number, or its type, and which one it does depends on its proliferative capacity. Labile tissues such as epidermis, gut, and bone marrow keep a dividing stem cell population and can add cells; stable tissues such as liver and kidney tubules divide only when stimulated; and permanent cells such as cardiac myocytes, skeletal myocytes, and neurons have left the cell cycle, so they can only enlarge.

Hypertrophy follows mechanical stretch or trophic signaling (growth factors, angiotensin II, alpha-adrenergic agonists) that increases synthesis of contractile protein, so each cell holds more sarcomeres. Hyperplasia follows growth factor or hormone stimulation of cells that can still divide, and in the epidermis the friction of a callus drives basal keratinocyte proliferation with thickening of the stratum corneum. The two often occur together, as in the estrogen-stimulated uterus. Atrophy is the reverse: reduced workload, denervation, ischemia, poor nutrition, loss of a trophic hormone, or pressure shifts the protein balance toward degradation, with ubiquitin tagging proteins for the proteasome and autophagy delivering organelles to lysosomes. Undigested membrane lipid from autophagy remains as lipofuscin, which is why atrophic organs often look brown.

Metaplasia replaces one mature epithelium with another that tolerates the stress better. The switch happens in stem or reserve cells reprogrammed by signals from the injured environment, not by transformation of a mature cell. Cigarette smoke replaces pseudostratified ciliated columnar bronchial epithelium with stratified squamous epithelium, which resists smoke but cannot clear mucus, so infection risk rises. Chronic acid reflux replaces distal esophageal squamous epithelium with intestinal-type columnar epithelium containing goblet cells (Barrett esophagus), which tolerates acid but carries a risk of adenocarcinoma.

blocks.title: The four adaptations compared
rows: More structural protein in cells that cannot divide
Left ventricle in hypertension; skeletal muscle in training
Growth factor or hormone drive on dividing cells
Callus; endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed estrogen
Reprogramming of stem or reserve cells
Squamous metaplasia of bronchi; Barrett esophagus
blocks.caption: All four are reversible while the stimulus lasts and then is removed; none of them involves genetic damage by itself.

blocks.text: The link to cancer is proliferation sustained over time. Every division risks a replication error, and persistent injury supplies both the mitogenic signal and the mutagen. Dysplasia is the result: atypical nuclei, mitoses above the basal layer, and loss of maturation from base to surface, all still behind an intact basement membrane. Whether an adaptation carries that risk depends on the stimulus, not on the word: pathologic hyperplasia from unopposed estrogen in the endometrium progresses to dysplasia and carcinoma, while benign prostatic hyperplasia and a callus do not.

blocks.title: From chronic injury to invasive carcinoma in the bronchus
steps: Smoke repeatedly injures ciliated columnar epithelium
Reserve cells are reprogrammed to squamous epithelium
Continued injury sustains proliferation; mutations accumulate
Dysplasia: atypia with loss of orientation
Carcinoma in situ: full-thickness atypia, basement membrane intact
Invasive squamous cell carcinoma breaches the basement membrane
blocks.caption: Metaplasia itself is reversible; the risk lies in the sustained proliferation that follows it.

blocks.predict: A sedentary patient begins weight training and a cyclist's calf is immobilized in a cast. Both muscles change size. Why does neither change involve a change in cell number?
blocks.explain: Skeletal muscle fibers are permanent cells that cannot re-enter the cell cycle, so added demand can only add sarcomeres (hypertrophy) and removed demand can only shift the protein balance toward ubiquitin-proteasome degradation and autophagy (atrophy). Satellite cells repair damage but do not expand the fiber population enough to count as hyperplasia.
blocks.check: The proliferative capacity categories in the first paragraph and the adaptations table.

sections.title: Mechanisms of cell injury and the reversible to irreversible transition

blocks.text: Most injuries converge on a small number of intracellular events: ATP depletion, mitochondrial damage, rising cytosolic calcium, oxidative stress, and membrane damage. Each one amplifies the others, which is why injury accelerates once it begins.

Hypoxia stops oxidative phosphorylation first, because the electron transport chain has no terminal electron acceptor. ATP falls, and the Na+/K+-ATPase slows, so sodium and water enter and the cell swells while potassium leaks out. The cell switches to anaerobic glycolysis, which consumes glycogen and generates lactate, lowering intracellular pH and clumping nuclear chromatin. Low ATP also releases calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum and allows ribosomes to detach from rough endoplasmic reticulum, so protein synthesis falls. Note the distinction between hypoxia, which is reduced oxygen delivery from any cause, and ischemia, which is reduced blood flow and therefore removes substrate and leaves waste behind as well. Ischemia injures faster than hypoxia alone for exactly that reason.

Cytosolic calcium is the central amplifier. Normally held near 0.1 micromolar against a millimolar extracellular concentration, it rises when ATP-dependent pumps fail and membranes leak. Calcium activates phospholipases that strip membrane phospholipid, proteases that cleave cytoskeletal and membrane proteins, endonucleases that fragment DNA, and ATPases that waste what little ATP remains. It also opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, which collapses the proton gradient and ends any chance of restoring ATP.

Oxidative stress arises from leaked electrons in the respiratory chain, from the respiratory burst of neutrophils, from ionizing and ultraviolet radiation, and from Fenton chemistry when free iron or copper is present. Superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, and vitamins C and E normally keep these species in check. When they are overwhelmed, hydroxyl radical initiates lipid peroxidation, a chain reaction that propagates along membranes, while protein oxidation inactivates enzymes and DNA oxidation produces strand breaks. Reperfusion is a special case: restoring oxygen to tissue with damaged mitochondria and primed neutrophils generates a burst of radicals and complement activation, so some cells die after flow returns rather than before.

blocks.title: Hypoxic cell injury step by step
steps: Oxidative phosphorylation stops; ATP falls
Na+/K+-ATPase fails; sodium and water enter; the cell swells
Anaerobic glycolysis raises lactate and lowers pH
Ribosomes detach; protein synthesis falls
Cytosolic calcium rises; degradative enzymes are activated
Permeability transition pore opens; ATP recovery becomes impossible
Membranes rupture; contents leak and inflammation follows
blocks.caption: Everything above the permeability transition pore is still reversible if perfusion returns; everything below it is not.

blocks.text: The point of no return is defined by two events: mitochondria that can no longer make ATP, and extensive membrane damage. Before that point the cell shows swelling (hydropic change), clear cytoplasmic vacuoles, surface blebbing, loss of microvilli, dilated endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondrial swelling, and fatty change where lipid accumulates because injured cells cannot export triglyceride. After it, the plasma membrane ruptures and cytosolic proteins enter the blood, which is why troponin rises only after myocytes are irreversibly injured rather than during reversible ischemia. Lysosomal rupture releases hydrolases that digest the cell, and the nucleus passes through pyknosis (shrunken, condensed chromatin), karyorrhexis (fragmentation), and karyolysis (dissolution by endonucleases) until no nucleus remains.

blocks.title: Reversible versus irreversible injury
rows: Increased eosinophilia from protein denaturation and RNA loss
Ruptured; enzymes such as troponin leak into blood
blocks.caption: Nuclear change and membrane rupture are the decisive findings; swelling and fatty change alone do not mean the cell is dead.

sections.title: Patterns of necrosis and the settings that produce them

blocks.text: Necrosis is the morphologic result of enzymatic digestion of a cell that has already died, and the pattern depends on which process wins: protein denaturation, which fixes structure in place, or hydrolytic digestion, which liquefies it. Hydrolases come from the dead cell itself (autolysis) or from recruited leukocytes (heterolysis), so the lysosome and leukocyte content of the setting predicts the pattern.

In coagulative necrosis, ischemic acidosis denatures structural proteins and lysosomal enzymes together, so digestion is delayed and the architecture is preserved for days: cells become firm, intensely eosinophilic, and anucleate with ghost outlines still recognizable, producing a wedge-shaped pale infarct in heart, kidney, spleen, or liver. In liquefactive necrosis, hydrolytic digestion dominates and the tissue becomes a viscous fluid. Two settings produce it: bacterial and some fungal infections, where neutrophils arrive in numbers and release their enzymes, and infarction of the central nervous system, where high lipid content, little fibrous stroma, and abundant neuronal and microglial lysosomal enzymes liquefy the tissue into a fluid-filled cyst. The brain is the standard exception to the rule that ischemia gives coagulative necrosis.

blocks.title: Patterns of necrosis
rows: Infarct of heart, kidney, spleen, or liver
Firm, pale, eosinophilic ghost cells without nuclei
Acidosis denatures enzymes, so architecture persists
Hydrolases from leukocytes or neural tissue digest the tissue
Crumbly cheese-like debris inside a granuloma
Lipid-rich cell wall plus granulomatous walling off
Lipase frees fatty acids that bind calcium (saponification)
Immune complexes plus fibrin deposited in the wall
Limb ischemia, usually a lower extremity
Dry mummified tissue, or swollen and foul if infected
Coagulative necrosis, with liquefaction added by bacteria
blocks.caption: Gangrene is a clinical term for coagulative necrosis of a limb, not a separate mechanism; wet gangrene is dry gangrene with superimposed bacterial liquefaction.

blocks.text: Caseous necrosis is a granulomatous variant in which the mycobacterial lipid-rich cell wall and the walling off by macrophages leave amorphous granular debris, neither fully preserved nor fully liquefied, surrounded by epithelioid macrophages and giant cells. Fat necrosis is enzymatic rather than ischemic: lipase released from pancreatic acinar cells hydrolyzes triglyceride in peripancreatic fat, and the liberated fatty acids combine with calcium to form soaps, a saponification visible as chalky white deposits and detectable as a fall in serum calcium. Fibrinoid necrosis is seen only microscopically, where immune complexes with plasma fibrin give the vessel wall a bright pink smudged appearance.

Each pattern has a time course that board questions exploit. Nuclear loss and eosinophilia in a myocardial infarct appear over roughly 4 to 12 hours, neutrophils peak at 1 to 3 days, macrophages clear debris over the following week, and granulation tissue and collagenous scar follow over weeks. Tissue that cannot regenerate heals by scar, so a healed cardiac infarct is fibrous while liquefied brain leaves a cyst bordered by glial scar, and debris that is not cleared becomes a site for dystrophic calcification.

blocks.title: Two infarcts, two patterns
blocks.text: An embolus occludes a branch of the left anterior descending artery, and a second embolus from the same left atrium occludes a middle cerebral artery branch. Both tissues die by the same mechanism of ATP depletion and calcium overload. Two days later the myocardium is a firm pale wedge of eosinophilic anucleate fibers whose outlines are still visible, surrounded by neutrophils, because ischemic acidosis denatured the lysosomal enzymes along with the structural proteins. The brain lesion is already softening, because neural tissue is lipid-rich, has little collagen stroma, and supplies abundant hydrolases. Same mechanism of death, different morphology, because the balance of denaturation against digestion differs.

sections.title: Apoptosis, cytotoxic killing, and how apoptosis differs from necrosis

blocks.text: Apoptosis is a programmed, ATP-requiring death in which the cell dismantles itself using caspases, cysteine proteases that cleave after aspartate residues. Initiator caspases (8, 9, and 10) head each pathway and activate executioner caspases (3, 6, and 7), which cleave cytoskeletal and nuclear matrix proteins and activate a DNase that cuts DNA between nucleosomes. The result is a shrunken cell with condensed chromatin whose membrane stays intact.

The intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway handles DNA damage, misfolded protein accumulation, and withdrawal of survival signals such as growth factors or hormones. It is governed at the outer mitochondrial membrane by the BCL-2 family: antiapoptotic members (BCL-2, BCL-XL, MCL1) hold the membrane closed, proapoptotic effectors BAX and BAK oligomerize to open it, and BH3-only sensors (BIM, BID, PUMA, NOXA, several induced by p53) tip the balance. Once the membrane is permeabilized, cytochrome c enters the cytosol, binds APAF-1 to form the apoptosome, and activates caspase-9. Overexpression of BCL-2, as in follicular lymphoma with the t(14;18) translocation, keeps the membrane shut so damaged cells survive.

blocks.title: Intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis
steps: DNA damage or loss of survival signals activates BH3-only sensors
The sensors neutralize BCL-2 and free BAX and BAK
BAX and BAK permeabilize the outer mitochondrial membrane
Cytochrome c reaches the cytosol and binds APAF-1
The apoptosome activates caspase-9
Caspases 3 and 7 cleave substrates and fragment DNA
Macrophages phagocytose apoptotic bodies; no inflammation
blocks.caption: The decision point is the BCL-2 to BAX and BAK balance at the mitochondrion, not the caspase cascade itself.

blocks.text: The extrinsic (death receptor) pathway begins outside the cell. Fas ligand on an activated T cell crosslinks Fas (CD95), or tumor necrosis factor binds TNF receptor 1, and the clustered death domains recruit adaptor proteins (FADD for Fas) that activate caspase-8. In cells with abundant caspase-8 this is enough; in others caspase-8 cleaves BID to a truncated form that engages the mitochondrial pathway, so the two routes amplify one another. The same system removes self-reactive lymphocytes, and inherited loss of Fas causes an autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.

Cytotoxic T lymphocytes and natural killer cells have a third route. Perforin polymerizes in the target membrane to deliver granzymes into the cytosol, and granzyme B cleaves and activates caspases directly, bypassing both the receptor and the mitochondrion. The same cells also express Fas ligand, so one lymphocyte can use either mechanism. All three routes converge on executioner caspases 3 and 7.

blocks.title: Apoptosis versus necrosis
rows: Pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis by random digestion
blocks.caption: The externalized phosphatidylserine is the eat-me signal; because nothing leaks, no danger signals reach the innate immune system.

blocks.text: The two deaths are not mutually exclusive. In one infarct, severely ischemic cells die by necrosis while marginal cells that retain some ATP die by apoptosis, and necroptosis blurs the boundary further. Apoptosis also runs physiologically: involution of embryonic structures, loss of hormone-dependent endometrium, keratinocyte death in sunburn, and deletion of self-reactive lymphocytes. When clearance of apoptotic cells fails, nuclear material persists and can drive antinuclear antibody formation, a mechanism relevant to lupus.

blocks.predict: A cell line lacking BAX and BAK is irradiated, then separately exposed to an activated cytotoxic T cell. In which case does it still die by apoptosis?
blocks.explain: It survives the radiation, because DNA damage signals through p53 and BH3-only proteins to BAX and BAK, and without those effectors the mitochondrion cannot release cytochrome c. The T cell still kills it, because granzyme B activates executioner caspases directly, bypassing the mitochondrion.
blocks.check: The intrinsic apoptosis flow and the paragraph on perforin and granzyme.

blocks.text: A pigment is colored material visible in tissue without staining. Endogenous pigments are synthesized or generated by the body, and each one records a specific process; exogenous pigments arrive from outside and persist because macrophages hold them.

Lipofuscin is the wear and tear pigment, a yellow-brown granular complex of peroxidized membrane lipid and protein that accumulates in lysosomes because it cannot be fully digested. It is not injurious in itself; it is a marker of long-standing free radical damage and lipid peroxidation, and so accumulates with age and with atrophy in heart, liver, and neurons. Gross brown discoloration of an atrophic heart is called brown atrophy. Melanin is the only endogenous brown-black pigment that is deliberately made: melanocytes polymerize tyrosine through tyrosinase into eumelanin and pheomelanin within melanosomes and transfer the melanosomes to keratinocytes, where the pigment caps the nucleus and absorbs ultraviolet radiation.

Hemosiderin is aggregated ferritin micelles, a golden-brown pigment that forms when iron exceeds the storage capacity of ferritin. Local excess follows hemorrhage: macrophages phagocytose extravasated red cells, degrade hemoglobin, and store the iron, which is why a bruise passes through red-blue (hemoglobin), then green-blue (biliverdin and bilirubin), then golden-brown (hemosiderin). Systemic excess from transfusion, hereditary hemochromatosis, or ineffective erythropoiesis deposits hemosiderin in liver, pancreas, heart, and skin. The Prussian blue (Perls) reaction converts the ferric iron to a blue ferric ferrocyanide, so iron appears blue and is distinguished from lipofuscin and melanin, which do not react. Bilirubin is the yellow-green product of heme catabolism, not an iron-containing pigment; when conjugation or excretion fails or hemolysis overwhelms the liver, it stains skin, sclera, and mucosae as jaundice, and in neonates unconjugated bilirubin can cross the immature blood-brain barrier to stain basal ganglia (kernicterus).

Bleaches with melanin bleach; positive for S100 and melan-A in cells
Yellow-green in skin, sclera, liver canaliculi
No iron; jaundice when serum level rises
Black in alveolar macrophages and hilar nodes
Inert unless dose is heavy enough for fibrosis
Variable, in dermal macrophages and fibroblasts
Persists for life; no inflammation unless allergic
blocks.caption: Hemosiderin, lipofuscin, and melanin all look brown on routine stain, so the iron stain and the clinical setting separate them.

blocks.text: Exogenous pigments are defined by where they lodge. Inhaled carbon is taken up by alveolar macrophages, carried along lymphatics, and concentrated in hilar and peribronchial lymph nodes, where blackened tissue constitutes anthracosis. In city dwellers the dose is low and the pigment is inert, while in coal workers the heavy dose provokes macrophage activation, fibrogenic cytokine release, and coal workers pneumoconiosis, which shows that an inert pigment becomes injurious at high dose. Tattoo ink is phagocytosed by dermal macrophages and fibroblasts that stay in place rather than migrating to nodes, so the pattern persists for life, with replacement macrophages taking up pigment released when an older cell dies. Delayed hypersensitivity to a pigment, classically red mercury-based inks, produces a localized granulomatous reaction.

blocks.title: Why a bruise changes color
steps: Red cells extravasate; hemoglobin gives red-purple
Macrophages phagocytose red cells and degrade hemoglobin
Heme oxygenase makes biliverdin, seen as green
Biliverdin is reduced to bilirubin, seen as yellow
Released iron exceeds ferritin and is stored as hemosiderin
Golden-brown hemosiderin remains and stains blue with Prussian blue
blocks.caption: The color sequence is a visible timeline of heme catabolism inside macrophages.

sections.title: Pathologic calcification and intracellular or extracellular infiltrates

blocks.text: Pathologic calcification is abnormal deposition of calcium salts, usually calcium phosphate in a hydroxyapatite-like crystal, sometimes with iron and other minerals. There are two forms, and serum calcium separates them.

Dystrophic calcification occurs in dead or dying tissue with a normal serum calcium. It begins when membrane phospholipids of damaged cells and shed membrane vesicles expose phosphate groups that bind calcium; phosphatases in the vesicles generate more phosphate, and the crystal propagates on a protein scaffold. Classic sites are atheromatous plaques, aging or damaged aortic and mitral valves, caseous necrosis in healed tuberculosis, old fat necrosis, and the laminated psammoma bodies of meningioma, papillary thyroid carcinoma, and serous ovarian tumors. Calcification is usually only a marker of previous injury, but in a valve cusp it stiffens the leaflet enough to cause stenosis.

Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissue when the serum calcium-phosphate product is raised, as in hyperparathyroidism (primary or secondary to renal failure), bone destruction from metastases or myeloma, vitamin D excess including granulomatous disease that converts vitamin D, and chronic kidney disease with phosphate retention. Deposits favor the interstitium of gastric mucosa, kidney (nephrocalcinosis), lung, systemic arteries, and pulmonary veins, because these tissues lose acid and so have a relatively alkaline internal environment in which calcium phosphate is less soluble.

blocks.title: Dystrophic versus metastatic calcification
rows: Phosphate on damaged membranes nucleates crystal
Local, at the site of injury
Atheroma, aged valves, caseous necrosis, psammoma bodies
Hyperparathyroidism, chronic kidney disease, vitamin D excess, myeloma
blocks.caption: The question to ask on a board item is whether the serum calcium is normal; if it is, the lesion came first and the calcium followed.

blocks.text: Infiltrates are substances that accumulate where they do not belong. Steatosis is triglyceride within parenchymal cells, most often hepatocytes, appearing as clear vacuoles that displace the nucleus. It occurs whenever fatty acid delivery or synthesis outstrips export: alcohol raises NADH and shifts metabolism toward fatty acid synthesis, insulin resistance raises fatty acid delivery from adipose tissue, and protein malnutrition, carbon tetrachloride, and some drugs block apolipoprotein synthesis. Steatosis is reversible, but sustained lipid loading produces oxidative stress and inflammation (steatohepatitis) that can proceed to fibrosis and cirrhosis.

Cholesterol accumulates in macrophages that have taken up modified lipoprotein and cannot export it, producing foam cells with abundant fine vacuoles. Foam cells populate the atheromatous plaque, cluster in dermis and tendons as xanthomas and in the eyelid as xanthelasma, and appear in the gallbladder wall as cholesterolosis. Amyloid is a different kind of deposit: not one substance but any of many proteins misfolded into a beta-pleated sheet fibril, including immunoglobulin light chains in plasma cell dyscrasia (AL), serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation (AA), beta-2 microglobulin in long-term dialysis, transthyretin in familial and senile forms, and islet amyloid polypeptide in type 2 diabetes. Because the fibril is regular and extracellular, Congo red aligns along the fibril axis and produces apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Amyloid causes disease by physically replacing tissue, so the heart stiffens, the kidney leaks protein, and the tongue and nerves enlarge.

blocks.title: How alcohol produces hepatic steatosis
steps: Ethanol oxidation generates excess NADH
High NADH inhibits fatty acid oxidation and favors synthesis
Acetate and acetyl-CoA feed triglyceride assembly
Lipoprotein assembly and export from the hepatocyte fall
Triglyceride accumulates as cytoplasmic vacuoles
Reversible with abstinence; sustained loading drives steatohepatitis
blocks.caption: Steatosis is an imbalance between fatty acid supply and triglyceride export, not a form of cell death.

sections.title: Benign and malignant neoplasms, naming, grade, and stage

blocks.text: A neoplasm is a clonal proliferation that has become independent of normal growth controls and continues after the initiating stimulus is gone. That autonomy separates it from hyperplasia, which stops when the stimulus stops. Its transformed parenchymal cells determine its behavior and name; its stroma of connective tissue and vessels is recruited.

Benign and malignant tumors differ along four lines: differentiation, growth rate, local invasion, and metastasis. Differentiation is how closely tumor cells resemble their normal counterpart, and anaplasia is the morphologic expression of losing it, listed in the table below. Growth rate generally tracks differentiation, so a fast-growing tumor may outstrip its blood supply and develop central necrosis. Malignant invasion is infiltrative, so there is no true capsule, while a benign tumor expands and compresses neighboring tissue into a fibrous rim that allows it to be shelled out. Metastasis is the one unequivocally malignant feature: no benign tumor metastasizes.

blocks.title: Benign versus malignant
rows: Anaplasia: pleomorphism, hyperchromatic coarse nuclei, prominent nucleoli, nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio toward 1 to 1 (normally 1 to 4 or 1 to 6), atypical mitoses, lost polarity, tumor giant cells
blocks.caption: Benign does not mean harmless: a meningioma compresses the brain and an insulinoma can cause fatal hypoglycemia.

blocks.text: Naming is the tissue of origin plus a suffix: -oma for a benign mesenchymal tumor, sarcoma for a malignant one, carcinoma for any malignant epithelial tumor, and papilloma, adenoma, or cystadenoma for benign epithelium by pattern. A mixed tumor shows divergent differentiation within one germ layer, as in pleomorphic adenoma, while a teratoma arises from more than one. A hamartoma is a disorganized but mature overgrowth of native tissue and a choristoma is normal tissue in the wrong place; neither is a true neoplasm.

blocks.title: Naming rules and exceptions
blocks.caption: Melanoma, lymphoma, myeloma, mesothelioma, and seminoma all end in -oma and are malignant.

blocks.text: Between normal epithelium and invasive cancer lies a graded sequence. Dysplasia is disordered growth with cytologic atypia, mitoses above the basal layer, and loss of orientation and surface maturation, and it is reversible if the stimulus is removed. When atypia occupies the full epithelial thickness but the basement membrane is intact, the lesion is carcinoma in situ, which cannot metastasize because no cell has reached a vessel. Invasion requires loss of E-cadherin adhesion and degradation of collagen IV and laminin by matrix metalloproteinases.

Grade and stage answer different questions. Grade is microscopic: how far the tumor has departed from its parent tissue, by differentiation, nuclear atypia, and mitotic count. Stage is anatomic: how far it has spread, by TNM, with T for size or depth of invasion, N for regional nodes, M for distant metastasis. Stage predicts outcome better in most solid tumors, because whether the tumor is still locally confined determines whether local control is possible. Carcinomas usually spread first through lymphatics, sarcomas hematogenously to lung.

blocks.predict: One colon biopsy shows full-thickness atypia with an intact basement membrane; another shows well differentiated glands that have crossed into the submucosa. Which patient needs node staging?
blocks.explain: The second. The first is carcinoma in situ and cannot have metastasized, because no cell has reached a lymphatic or venule. The second has invaded, so despite its lower grade it can seed nodes, and stage carries more prognostic weight.

sections.title: Hallmarks of cancer and the genes behind them

blocks.text: Carcinogenesis is a multistep accumulation of genetic and epigenetic change in one cell lineage, involving four classes of gene: proto-oncogenes, whose gain of function drives growth; tumor suppressors, whose loss removes brakes; apoptosis regulators; and DNA repair genes.

Self-sufficiency in growth signals comes from activating mutations anywhere along a growth factor pathway. A single substitution in BRAF, valine to glutamate at position 600, locks the kinase in its active conformation so the MAP kinase cascade signals without an upstream growth factor. The same mutation is present in most common acquired nevi as well as in a large share of melanomas, which shows that one activating mutation is not sufficient for cancer. RAS mutations prevent GTP hydrolysis and leave RAS GTP-bound, and MYC amplification drives cell cycle transcription. Because one mutant allele already makes a signaling protein, oncogenes act dominantly.

Insensitivity to growth inhibition comes from losing tumor suppressors, and because one normal allele still makes enough protein, both copies must be lost: the two-hit requirement. In hereditary retinoblastoma the first hit is inherited, so tumors are early and often bilateral, while sporadic cases need both hits in one somatic cell. Unphosphorylated RB binds E2F and holds the cell at the G1 to S restriction point, and cyclin D with CDK4 or CDK6 phosphorylates RB to release E2F, so cyclin D amplification, loss of p16, and loss of RB all leave that checkpoint unguarded. TP53 induces p21 to arrest the cell in G1 for repair and proapoptotic proteins such as PUMA when repair fails, so losing both alleles removes arrest and apoptotic backup together.

blocks.title: Hallmarks and genes
rows: Gain of function in a growth pathway
PD-L1; loss of MHC class I
Mismatch repair loss; BRCA1 and BRCA2
blocks.caption: Most tumors acquire several of these, which is why single-gene explanations fall short.

blocks.text: Three hallmarks deserve a mechanistic note. Telomeres shorten with each division and once critically short trigger p53-dependent senescence, so telomerase reactivation makes a lineage effectively immortal. Angiogenesis is required because diffusion supports a cell mass only to roughly 1 to 2 mm, so hypoxia stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha, which transcribes VEGF. Warburg metabolism favors glycolysis with lactate even when oxygen is available: less ATP per glucose, but a rapid supply of carbon skeletons for nucleotides and lipids.

Genomic instability is the accelerator rather than a capability: losing a repair gene raises the mutation rate genome-wide, so oncogene activation and suppressor loss arrive faster. The immune system is the outer constraint. Tumor antigens appear on MHC class I and are recognized by cytotoxic T cells, which is why immunocompromised patients develop more malignancies. Tumors escape by downregulating MHC class I (leaving them vulnerable to natural killer cells), losing the antigen, recruiting regulatory T cells, and expressing PD-L1, which engages PD-1 and switches off the T cell.

blocks.title: Why a nevus with BRAF V600E stays a nevus
blocks.text: A melanocyte acquires BRAF V600E, so MAP kinase signaling runs without a growth factor and the cell divides to form a nevus. Sustained signaling then induces p16 and engages the p53 pathway while telomeres shorten, so the clone enters oncogene-induced senescence, which is why most nevi are stable for decades. Progression needs further events: loss of p16 or RB to release the G1 checkpoint, TP53 loss or BCL-2 excess to evade apoptosis, telomerase, and VEGF-driven vessels. A growth advantage is not malignancy.

integration.text: The sequence in this chapter is one continuous story read at different magnifications. Biochemistry sets the first step, because every injury pathway runs through ATP supply, calcium gradients, and the balance between radical production and the antioxidant defenses of superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, and vitamins C and E. Histology and anatomy decide what the injury looks like, which is why the same ischemic death produces a firm pale wedge in the heart and a liquefied cyst in the brain, and why the lipid-rich mycobacterial wall gives caseous rather than liquefactive debris. Immunology supplies both the executioners and the brakes: Fas ligand, TNF, and perforin with granzyme are immune routes into the caspase cascade, while PD-L1 and loss of MHC class I are how a tumor turns that same system off.

Pathology then reads the record backward, and that is the reasoning board questions ask for. A brown pigment plus a positive Prussian blue reaction means iron and therefore a previous hemorrhage or iron overload; the same brown color without iron in an atrophic heart means lipofuscin and therefore years of lipid peroxidation. Calcium in damaged tissue with a normal serum calcium points to a local injury that has already happened, while calcium in normal tissue points to a systemic problem of calcium and phosphate handling. Apple-green birefringence under polarized light means a beta-pleated fibril, and the clinical setting then names which protein. The limits are worth stating plainly: morphology gives a pattern, not a cause, several processes can produce the same appearance, and the timing of changes after an injury varies with tissue and with the patient, so the microscope is read together with the history and the laboratory values.

summary: Which adaptation a stressed cell shows depends on whether it can divide: permanent cells only hypertrophy, labile cells can also undergo hyperplasia, and stem cell reprogramming produces metaplasia.
Metaplasia and pathologic hyperplasia carry cancer risk because the stimulus sustains proliferation, and dysplasia then develops behind an intact basement membrane.

Injury converges on ATP depletion, mitochondrial failure, calcium overload, and oxidative damage, and calcium is the amplifier that activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and the permeability transition pore.
Cell swelling and fatty change are reversible; membrane rupture with enzyme leakage and the nuclear changes pyknosis, karyorrhexis, and karyolysis are not.

The necrosis pattern reflects whether denaturation or digestion dominates: coagulative in infarcts of heart, kidney, and spleen, liquefactive in brain infarcts and abscesses, caseous in tuberculosis, enzymatic fat necrosis in pancreatitis, and fibrinoid in immune vasculitis.

Intrinsic apoptosis is decided by the BCL-2 to BAX and BAK balance, releasing cytochrome c to activate caspase-9; extrinsic apoptosis uses Fas or TNF receptor 1 to activate caspase-8, and granzyme B activates caspases directly.
Apoptosis shrinks a single cell, keeps the membrane intact, and causes no inflammation, while necrosis swells groups of cells, ruptures them, and provokes inflammation.

Prussian blue identifies hemosiderin, lipofuscin marks chronic lipid peroxidation, exogenous carbon concentrates in alveolar macrophages and hilar nodes, and Congo red with apple-green birefringence identifies amyloid.
Dystrophic calcification lands on damaged tissue with a normal serum calcium; metastatic calcification lands on normal tissue because the calcium-phosphate product is raised.

Metastasis alone proves malignancy, carcinoma in situ cannot metastasize because the basement membrane is intact, and stage predicts outcome better than grade because oncogene gain, two-hit suppressor loss, apoptosis evasion, telomerase, angiogenesis, and immune evasion must all be in place before a tumor spreads.

The normal resting cytosolic free calcium concentration is quoted from about 0.05 to 0.2 micromolar in different texts; about 0.1 micromolar is used here.

Timing of morphologic change after myocardial infarction varies between sources (nuclear loss and eosinophilia from about 4 to 12 hours, neutrophil peak at 1 to 3 days); confirm the intervals NABNE expects if timing is tested.
The maximum tissue mass supported by diffusion before angiogenesis is required is quoted from about 1 to 2 mm in most sources; some give up to 2 to 3 mm.
The reported frequency of BRAF V600E in melanoma varies by series (roughly 40% to 60%) and is high in common acquired nevi; this chapter gives no single figure.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Perls reaction, Barrett esophagus, Li-Fraumeni syndrome, Lynch syndrome, and Warburg effect, or only the descriptive mechanisms.
Whether necroptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis are within the scope of Part I is unclear; they are mentioned here only as evidence that the apoptosis and necrosis boundary is not absolute.
Normal nuclear to cytoplasmic ratios (about 1 to 4 or 1 to 6 in differentiated cells) are approximate and differ by cell type; the point of the comparison is the shift toward 1 to 1 in anaplasia.
